chunks: Routing the buck feedback network. The question: How should you route the sense/feedback network of a buck converter?
The feedback network of a buck converter is two resistors that shrink the output voltage to a small sample.
The chip compares that sample with a fixed reference to keep the output steady. The sample point is easy to disturb, because a tiny leaked current can move it a lot.
So you put the resistors right at the chip's feedback pin, keep the junction short, and keep it away from noisy parts.
Picture a very sensitive microphone placed next to a drum kit. A gentle tap on a drum comes through as a loud bang.
Here the drums are the switch node and the inductor, and the faint signal is the feedback junction.
A tiny capacitance C c from the switch node injects a step into the tap, divided against the pin capacitance C p . The divider's Thevenin resistance (7.
6 kilohms) then sets how fast the step decays: tau equals 7. 6 kilohms times 5. 1 picofarads about 39 nanoseconds.
Feedback (FB) pin: the chip pin that watches the sample of the output voltage. Voltage divider: two resistors in series that output a fixed fraction of the input.
Reference voltage: a fixed voltage inside the chip, here 0. 8 volts, that the FB pin is held to.
Capacitance: how strongly two nearby pieces of metal pass fast voltage changes to each other. 1 picofarads is a trillionth of a farad.
High-impedance node: a point that a very small current can push around. Switch node: where the converter's switches meet the inductor, jumping between 0 volts and the input.
A 31. 6 kilohms resistor over a 10 kilohms resistor turns 3. 3 volts into about 0. 8 volts, matching the reference. Now say a stray 0.
1 picofarads links the switch node to the FB pin, which has about 5 picofarads of its own. A 12 volts edge splits between the two capacitances, so the pin jumps by 12 times 0.
1 / 5. 1 = about 0. 24 volts . That is a big jump on a 0. 8 volts pin. That is the whole idea: keep the delicate junction short and far from noise.

"The feedback divider is the most sensitive node, so I put it right at the FB pin with the high-impedance tap only a few millimetres long, its bottom resistor on the quiet analog ground, and the whole thing on the far side of the IC from the switch node and inductor.
Any long run goes on the low-impedance sense line from the output, taken after the output capacitors at the load. I never route it under or beside the inductor, because even 0.
1 picofarads from the switch node puts about 0. 24 volts on the pin."
